metadata.title: Pearl's Ladder: Correlation Dressed as Causation
metadata.topic: INFO 7375 REALLOCATION ENGINE, AUDITED — PEARL'S LADDER (E4/6)
metadata.playlist: The Tool That Doubts Itself — The Reallocation Engine, Audited
metadata.source: INFO 7375 (Computational Skepticism for AI) — The Reallocation Engine, Audited: Build a Useful Tool That Doubts Itself (100 pts)

beats.narration_text: Annyeong — Liam, in for Bear. Episode 4 of 6, and this is the one the assignment calls its heart: fifteen points, the highest-weighted component on the rubric. Here is why it deserves that weight. Every reallocation is a causal claim in disguise. When your engine says move the resource to B, it is not describing the data — it is asserting that moving the resource to B will CAUSE a better outcome. Your model was trained on observations. The claim is about an intervention. The entire component is the distance between those two sentences. Pearl's ladder gives the distance three rungs: seeing, doing, imagining. Today we climb all three with your engine, name the confounders on the way up, and then answer the question most students flinch from: is this engine reallocating on correlation dressed as causation? Spoiler from the rubric itself: most do — and honesty about it outscores a false claim of causal validity. Let's climb.

props.topic: INFO 7375 REALLOCATION ENGINE, AUDITED — PEARL'S LADDER (E4/6)
props.segment: Pearl's Ladder: Correlation Dressed as Causation
props.command: Climb all three rungs: what correlates (seeing) — what changes under intervention (doing) — what would have happened (imagining). Name the confounders. Deliver the honest verdict.
props.runningText: every reallocation is a causal claim in disguise — trained on observations, asserting an intervention…
output: 15 points — the highest-weighted component on the rubric
The graded question: correlation dressed as causation? (Most engines: yes. Honesty outscores pretense.)

beats.narration_text: Rung one: observation. Seeing. The question at this rung is the only question your training data can actually answer: what correlates with a good outcome? Campaigns with higher last-month ROI correlate with higher next-month bookings. Units with more staff correlate with fewer incidents. Warehouses with faster turnover correlate with fewer stockouts. Write your engine's version of that sentence down, because being precise at rung one is what makes the next two rungs sharp. And be honest about what your model IS at this rung: every regression, every gradient-boosted tree, every neural ranker — no matter how sophisticated — is a rung-one machine. It estimates the probability of a good outcome GIVEN that the resource was where it was. Given. Conditioned on. Observed alongside. That is association, and association is genuinely useful — it narrows the world, it flags candidates, it prices patterns. What it cannot do, even in principle, is tell you what happens when YOU change where the resource goes. The data was generated by a world with its own allocation process; your model learned that world. The moment you reallocate, you replace that process — and rung one has nothing to say about the world you just created. That is not a flaw in your model. It is the definition of the rung it lives on.

lines: P(good outcome | resource was there) — seeing, not doing
The only question training data answers: what correlates with a good outcome?
Every model — regression to neural ranker — is a rung-one machine.

beats.act: rung two — doing, and the confounders
beats.narration_text: Rung two: intervention. Doing. The question changes shape: not what correlates, but what would change if you actually moved the resource. In Pearl's notation, the difference between P of outcome given allocation, and P of outcome given DO allocation — and that one word, do, is where engines quietly commit fraud. Ask it about your engine directly: is the quantity it optimizes interventional, or observational? Here is the test that exposes it — name the confounders. A confounder is anything that drives both where the resource currently sits and how good the outcomes look. The campaign with stellar ROI: seasonality drove both the spend and the returns — move budget there in Q1 and the correlation evaporates. The heavily staffed unit with great outcomes: it is the unit with the easy cases — that is WHY it got the staff. Give the hard-case unit more staff and outcomes will not match the projection, because staffing was never the only thing different. The high-turnover warehouse sits near the demand it seems to create. List yours. Every one you name is a specific mechanism by which your rung-one correlation could vanish under intervention. The rubric grades exactly this: confounders NAMED, not gestured at. 'There may be confounding' is worth nothing. 'Seasonality drives both spend and ROI in my data, and here is the seam in the March numbers' — that is the component doing its job.

lines: P(outcome | do(allocation)) — the word 'do' is the fraud line
Not what correlates — what CHANGES if you move the resource.
The test: name what drives both current allocation AND observed outcomes.

beats.act: rung three — imagining, and the honest verdict
beats.narration_text: Rung three: counterfactual. Imagining. Take one specific past case from your data — one week, one campaign, one shift — and answer: what would have happened had the engine reallocated differently? Not in general. That case. 'In the week of March 10th, the engine would have moved two nurses from unit A to unit B. Had it done so, we estimate incidents in A would have risen by X and fallen in B by Y.' Then the part that separates rigor from fan fiction: state the assumptions that counterfactual rests on. No spillover between units. Outcomes respond to staffing the same way in both directions. Nothing else about that week changes. Each assumption is a place your counterfactual can be wrong, and saying them out loud is the assignment. Then, the verdict. One plain sentence: does your engine reallocate on correlation dressed as causation? The rubric telegraphs the answer — most do — and it prices honesty explicitly. All three rungs, confounders named, honest verdict: fifteen. Observation only, causation assumed: eight. Correlation reported as cause with no interrogation: five or less, plus a minus-ten deduction. Read that pricing again. A truthful 'my engine is rung-one and here is exactly why its recommendation may not survive the intervention' beats a confident lie by seven points before the deduction even lands. The course is paying you to be honest. Take the money.

lines: One specific past case , stated assumptions , one plain sentence
One case: this week, this campaign, this shift
State the assumptions: no spillover , symmetric response , nothing else changes.

beats.narration_text: Verdict for Pearl's Ladder. A reallocation is a causal claim wearing a recommendation's clothes: move it to B and outcomes improve. Rung one is what your model actually does — it learned the correlations of a world whose allocation process your engine intends to replace. Rung two asks what survives the replacement, and the confounders you can name — seasonality, case mix, the reason the resource was already where it was — are the specific mechanisms by which the answer becomes 'not this correlation.' Rung three commits to one past case, one alternate move, and the assumptions holding that story up. And the verdict sentence is graded on honesty, not on flattery: most engines reallocate on correlation dressed as causation, and saying so precisely is worth more than every confident overclaim. Fifteen points for the truth, told with mechanisms. Next episode: break the engine on purpose, then bolt on the gate that stops it from moving anything unattended.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. The prompt to paste into Claude reads: My engine's top-ranked reallocation is: state the move — quantity, from, to. It is driven by this observed relationship: name the feature and the outcome it correlates with. List every confounder that could make this correlation vanish under intervention — anything that plausibly drives both where the resource currently sits and how good the outcomes look — ranked by plausibility in my domain. Then tell me which rung of Pearl's ladder my objective function actually optimizes, and defend the answer against my pushback. Why this is the one to run: confounder-hunting is a breadth game, and Claude's breadth is real — it will surface candidates you did not consider. But ranking them by plausibility is a domain-knowledge game, and that is yours. Fight the ranking. Push back on its rung diagnosis and make it defend the claim — the argument is where your Rung-2 section writes itself. And notice what you are doing: using the tool to interrogate the tool's own causal standing. If the AI convinces you your engine is rung one — and it probably is — you have just earned the most honest sentence in your report. Write it down before the feeling fades.
